title: A Water Bottle Tied the Boston Strangler Confession to One Murder

narration: A man confessed to being the Boston Strangler.
For decades, many doubted him.
Then someone threw a water bottle away.
shots.visual_description: bs16 boston 1960s (night grade); bs16_desalvo (silhouette): stand -> hands_together -> bowed; bs16_desalvo (silhouette): stand (walks); bs16_detective (silhouette): stand -> arms_crossed -> bowed -> arms_crossed -> point; camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: label 'BOSTON · 1962-1964', callout 'THE WATER BOTTLE'.

overlays.text: THE WATER BOTTLE

sources.claim_text: In 1965, while already in custody on other charges, Albert DeSalvo confessed to the Strangler killings (to a psychiatrist and, through his lawyer F. Lee Bailey, in tape-recorded sessions with investigators).

For decades many doubted the confession: no physical evidence tied him to the killings, critics argued he could have learned the details elsewhere, he later recanted, and Mary Sullivan's nephew wrote a book arguing he was not her killer.

Detectives (a Boston Police fugitive-squad detective) secretly followed DeSalvo's male relatives until one, a nephew who was not named, drank from and threw away a water bottle, which the detective retrieved. The relative is never named or shown in this episode.

narration: From 1962 to 1964, thirteen women were killed around Boston.

sources.claim_text: Thirteen women were killed in and around Boston between 1962 and 1964 in the killings attributed to the 'Boston Strangler'. (Some reports count 11 or 14; 13 is the most common count.) No victim other than Mary Sullivan is named; no method is described.

narration: In 1965, Albert DeSalvo confessed to the killings.

Hollywood still made it a movie, twice.

sources.claim_text: DeSalvo was never tried (never charged) for any of the Strangler killings, for lack of physical evidence.

FUN FACT: Tony Curtis played DeSalvo in the 1968 film The Boston Strangler (dir. Richard Fleischer, 20th Century-Fox); in 2023 Keira Knightley played reporter Loretta McLaughlin in Boston Strangler (Hulu).

narration: He got life in prison for other crimes, and took back his confession.
In 1973, he was killed in prison.
shots.visual_description: courtroom (warm grade); judge: sit -> gavel -> sit -> read; bs16_desalvo (silhouette): stand -> stand_tense -> bowed; camera push/pull; overlays: card 'JANUARY 1967 / LIFE IN PRISON / FOR OTHER CRIMES / THEN HE RECANTED', label 'NOVEMBER 1973'.

overlays.text: JANUARY 1967 / LIFE IN PRISON / FOR OTHER CRIMES / THEN HE RECANTED
NOVEMBER 1973

sources.claim_text: In January 1967 DeSalvo was convicted of unrelated armed robberies and sexual assaults (the 'Green Man' case) and sentenced to life in prison; he later recanted his Strangler confession.
DeSalvo was killed in Walpole State Prison in November 1973 (no method is narrated or shown).

narration: The last victim was Mary Sullivan, just nineteen.
Even her family doubted him.
shots.visual_description: task force (cold grade); analyst: sit_read -> sit -> sit_read; bs16_detective: stand -> point_up -> bowed -> arms_crossed; keyed camera moves, handheld; overlays: card 'BOSTON · JANUARY 1964 / MARY SULLIVAN, 19 / THE LAST VICTIM', funfact 'In 2003, her nephew wrote / a whole book arguing / DeSalvo did NOT kill her.'.

sources.claim_text: Mary Sullivan, 19, killed in Boston in January 1964, is considered the last (final) victim. She is named only, never depicted.

FUN FACT: Mary Sullivan's nephew, author Casey Sherman, wrote A Rose for Mary (2003), arguing that DeSalvo was not her killer; DA Dan Conley said in 2013 that questions Mary's family had asked for almost 50 years had been answered.

narration: Police still had evidence from her case, but none of his DNA.
shots.visual_description: lab (cold grade); scientist: examine -> read -> stand; camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: card 'THE SULLIVAN CASE · 1964 / EVIDENCE KEPT FOR DECADES / DeSALVO'S DNA: NO SAMPLE'.

overlays.text: THE SULLIVAN CASE · 1964 / EVIDENCE KEPT FOR DECADES / DeSALVO'S DNA: NO SAMPLE

sources.claim_text: Police preserved evidence from the Sullivan case for almost 50 years; earlier attempts to get a usable DNA profile failed until a lab salvaged one in 2012; investigators had no usable DNA sample from DeSalvo.

narration: So detectives secretly followed his relatives.
One threw away a water bottle.
A detective picked it up.

sources.claim_text: Detectives (a Boston Police fugitive-squad detective) secretly followed DeSalvo's male relatives until one, a nephew who was not named, drank from and threw away a water bottle, which the detective retrieved. The relative is never named or shown in this episode.
DeSalvo's family, through lawyer Elaine Sharp, disputed the conclusion and objected to the covert collection of a relative's DNA; DA Conley called the method fair, legal and ethical.

narration: Its DNA was a familial match to evidence from Mary Sullivan's case.
shots.visual_description: lab (cold grade); examiner: examine -> read -> stand -> point; camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: card 'ANNOUNCED JULY 2013 / A FAMILIAL MATCH / SHARED BY MALE RELATIVES / NOT YET HIS OWN DNA'.

overlays.text: ANNOUNCED JULY 2013 / A FAMILIAL MATCH / SHARED BY MALE RELATIVES / NOT YET HIS OWN DNA

sources.claim_text: DNA from the bottle was a 'familial' (Y-chromosome) match to evidence from the Sullivan case, announced on 11 July 2013; the DA called it strong but not enough on its own to close the case with absolute certainty, and sought DeSalvo's exhumation.

narration: To be sure, they exhumed DeSalvo's remains.
Officials said it left no doubt he killed Mary Sullivan.

shots.reconstruction_tag: ILLUSTRATION · GENERIC CEMETERY, NO REMAINS SHOWN

sources.claim_text: DeSalvo's remains were exhumed (court-ordered, July 2013) and his DNA tested; on 19 July 2013 officials announced a match (odds of another white male put at one in 220 billion), and Attorney General Martha Coakley said it 'leaves no doubt' that he was responsible for Mary Sullivan's murder.

narration: But it links him to her murder only.
Whether he killed all thirteen is still debated.
shots.visual_description: press room (cold grade); official: read -> stand -> read; agent_a (silhouette): stand -> stand_tense -> stand; camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: card 'WHAT THE DNA SHOWS / MARY SULLIVAN'S MURDER / ONLY', card 'ALL THIRTEEN? / STILL DEBATED / His family disputed the result'.

sources.claim_text: The DNA links DeSalvo to Mary Sullivan's murder only; authorities said no DNA survives from the other cases, and whether one man (DeSalvo) committed all the killings is still debated.
DeSalvo's family, through lawyer Elaine Sharp, disputed the conclusion and objected to the covert collection of a relative's DNA; DA Conley called the method fair, legal and ethical.

narration: Her nephew called the result full justice for his aunt.
Remember the thirteen women.

sources.claim_text: Casey Sherman, Mary Sullivan's nephew, who had long argued DeSalvo was innocent, accepted the 2013 result and called it 'full justice for my aunt'.

Thirteen women were killed in and around Boston between 1962 and 1964 in the killings attributed to the 'Boston Strangler'. (Some reports count 11 or 14; 13 is the most common count.) No victim other than Mary Sullivan is named; no method is described.

narration: For Mary Sullivan, decades of doubt ended with one water bottle.

Next case tease: in December 2022 FBI agents collected trash the Kohberger family set out at their Pennsylvania home; DNA from it indicated the father of the person whose DNA was on a knife sheath at the Idaho crime scene.
